claim: Formins play an important role in the polymerization of unbranched actin filaments.
source: Formins play an important role in the polymerization of unbranched actin filaments, and particular formins slow elongation by 5–95%.
evidence: This is a general statement about formin function that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Particular formins slow elongation by 5–95%.
source: Formins play an important role in the polymerization of unbranched actin filaments, and particular formins slow elongation by 5–95%.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the range of elongation inhibition by formins, supported by established literature.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations revealed two factors that influence actin filament elongation and correlate with the rates of elongation.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations revealed two factors that influence actin filament elongation and correlate with the rates of elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulations performed in this study.

claim: FH2 domains can sterically block the addition of new actin subunits.
source: First, FH2 domains can sterically block the addition of new actin subunits.
evidence: This is a finding from the molecular dynamics simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: FH2 domains flatten the helical twist of the terminal actin subunits, making the end less favorable for subunit addition.
source: Second, FH2 domains flatten the helical twist of the terminal actin subunits, making the end less favorable for subunit addition.
evidence: This is a finding from the molecular dynamics simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Coarse-grained simulations over longer time scales support the conclusions from all-atom simulations.
source: Coarse-grained simulations over longer time scales support these conclusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the coarse-grained simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The simulations show that filaments spend time in states that either allow or block elongation.
source: The simulations show that filaments spend time in states that either allow or block elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rate of elongation is a time-average of the degree to which the formin compromises subunit addition rather than the formin-actin complex literally being in 'open' or 'closed' states.
source: The rate of elongation is a time-average of the degree to which the formin compromises subunit addition rather than the formin-actin complex literally being in 'open' or 'closed' states.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the simulation data and represents a key conclusion of the study.

claim: Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells.
source: Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells and is important for numerous functions regulated by interactions with many other proteins (Pollard and Cooper, 2009; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Blanchoin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology, supported by citations.

claim: Actin is important for numerous functions regulated by interactions with many other proteins.
source: Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells and is important for numerous functions regulated by interactions with many other proteins (Pollard and Cooper, 2009; Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Blanchoin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The dynamic actin network in the cell cortex enables cells to maintain specific shapes in addition to supporting the plasma membrane.
source: The dynamic actin network in the cell cortex enables cells to maintain specific shapes in addition to supporting the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin function in cells.

claim: Actin filaments in lamellipodia drive cellular movements.
source: Actin filaments in lamellipodia drive cellular movements, and contractile rings of actin filaments are responsible for cytokinesis (Chesarone et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Contractile rings of actin filaments are responsible for cytokinesis.
source: Actin filaments in lamellipodia drive cellular movements, and contractile rings of actin filaments are responsible for cytokinesis (Chesarone et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Transitions of actin between monomeric and filamentous states is a key feature of dynamic actin systems.
source: Transitions of actin between monomeric and filamentous states is a key feature of these dynamic systems (Pollard and Cooper, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Formins regulate actin assembly by nucleating and directing the elongation of unbranched actin filaments.
source: Formins regulate actin assembly by nucleating and directing the elongation of unbranched actin filaments (Grikscheit and Grosse, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about formin function supported by citation.

claim: Formin malfunctions are associated with cancer.
source: Formin malfunctions are associated with cancer (Favaro et al., 2006; Favaro et al., 2003; Lizárraga et al., 2009; Sahai and Marshall, 2002) and immune disorders (Colucci-Guyon et al., 2005), so characterizing formins is crucial for understanding these important diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Formin malfunctions are associated with immune disorders.
source: Formin malfunctions are associated with cancer (Favaro et al., 2006; Favaro et al., 2003; Lizárraga et al., 2009; Sahai and Marshall, 2002) and immune disorders (Colucci-Guyon et al., 2005), so characterizing formins is crucial for understanding these important diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Characterizing formins is crucial for understanding cancer and immune disorders.
source: Formin malfunctions are associated with cancer (Favaro et al., 2006; Favaro et al., 2003; Lizárraga et al., 2009; Sahai and Marshall, 2002) and immune disorders (Colucci-Guyon et al., 2005), so characterizing formins is crucial for understanding these important diseases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association between formin malfunctions and diseases.

claim: FH2 domain self-associates in a head-to-tail manner to form a homodimer that stabilizes actin filament nuclei.
source: Formins consist of multiple domains, including a conserved formin homology 2 (FH2) domain that self-associates in a head-to-tail manner to form a homodimer that stabilizes actin filament nuclei (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FH2 domain structure and function.

claim: FH2 dimers stay processively associated with the filament's barbed end by 'stepping' onto actin subunits as they incorporate into the growing filament.
source: FH2 dimers stay processively associated with the filament's barbed end by 'stepping' onto actin subunits as they incorporate into the growing filament.
evidence: This is established knowledge about formin processivity.

claim: FH1 domains are located directly N-terminal to the FH2 domain.
source: FH1 domains are located directly N-terminal to the FH2 domain and consist of flexible regions connecting multiple polyproline tracks that each bind a profilin-actin complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about formin domain organization.

claim: FH1 domains consist of flexible regions connecting multiple polyproline tracks that each bind a profilin-actin complex.
source: FH1 domains are located directly N-terminal to the FH2 domain and consist of flexible regions connecting multiple polyproline tracks that each bind a profilin-actin complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FH1 domain structure and function.

claim: Diffusive motions of the FH1 domains allow actin to transfer rapidly onto the barbed end.
source: Diffusive motions of the FH1 domains allow actin to transfer rapidly onto the barbed end.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FH1 domain function.

claim: Actin filament barbed ends associated with a formin FH2 domain elongate slower than free barbed ends.
source: Actin filament barbed ends associated with a formin FH2 domain elongate slower than free barbed ends (Paul and Pollard, 2009a; Kovar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The effect of formins slowing elongation is considered to arise from 'gating,' a rapid equilibrium between an 'open state' and a 'closed state'.
source: This effect is considered to arise from 'gating,' a rapid equilibrium between an 'open state' (when an actin subunit can bind the barbed end) and a 'closed state' (when the barbed end is blocked) (Paul and Pollard, 2009a; Kovar et al., 2006; Vavylonis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an established model in the field supported by citations.

claim: The fraction of time that a barbed end is in an 'open' state is defined as the gating factor.
source: The fraction of time that a barbed end is in an 'open' state is defined as the gating factor, which ranges from ~0.95 for mammalian formin mDia1 to ~0.5–0.7 for budding yeast formin Bni1 and to ~0.05 for fission yeast formin Cdc12 (Kovar et al., 2006; Harris et al., 2006; Moseley and Goode, 2005).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: The gating factor ranges from ~0.95 for mammalian formin mDia1 to ~0.5–0.7 for budding yeast formin Bni1 and to ~0.05 for fission yeast formin Cdc12.
source: The fraction of time that a barbed end is in an 'open' state is defined as the gating factor, which ranges from ~0.95 for mammalian formin mDia1 to ~0.5–0.7 for budding yeast formin Bni1 and to ~0.05 for fission yeast formin Cdc12 (Kovar et al., 2006; Harris et al., 2006; Moseley and Goode, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: Barbed ends with mDia1 are mostly in an 'open' state that does not slow elongation.
source: Thus, barbed ends with mDia1 are mostly in an 'open' state that does not slow elongation, while barbed ends with Cdc12 are mostly closed, strongly inhibiting elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gating factor measurements cited.

claim: Barbed ends with Cdc12 are mostly closed, strongly inhibiting elongation.
source: Thus, barbed ends with mDia1 are mostly in an 'open' state that does not slow elongation, while barbed ends with Cdc12 are mostly closed, strongly inhibiting elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gating factor measurements cited.

claim: Rapid transfer of actin from FH1 domains onto open barbed ends allows filaments to elongate rapidly, in spite of gating.
source: Rapid transfer of actin from FH1 domains onto open barbed ends allows filaments to elongate rapidly, in spite of gating (Chang et al., 1997; Courtemanche and Pollard, 2012; Paul et al., 2008; Watanabe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two mechanisms are proposed for formins to gate the barbed end.
source: Two mechanisms are proposed for formins to gate the barbed end (Paul and Pollard, 2009b; Otomo et al., 2005; Pring et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2004; Goode and Eck, 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of existing models in the literature supported by citations.

claim: In a closed state, the formin might sterically interfere with the incoming actin subunit.
source: In a closed state, the formin might sterically interfere with the incoming actin subunit and/or distort the barbed end of the filament to compromise binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the literature.

claim: In a closed state, the formin might distort the barbed end of the filament to compromise binding.
source: In a closed state, the formin might sterically interfere with the incoming actin subunit and/or distort the barbed end of the filament to compromise binding.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from the literature.

claim: An open state is assumed to have no steric interference from the FH2 domain to an incoming monomer binding between the terminal and penultimate subunits.
source: An open state is assumed to have no steric interference from the FH2 domain to an incoming monomer binding between the terminal and penultimate subunits (A2 and A3 in the nomenclature in Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an assumption from existing models in the literature.

claim: Some models assume that an open end of the filament has the natural 167° helical twist that is favorable for adding a subunit.
source: Some (Paul et al., 2008; Paul and Pollard, 2009b) but not all (Otomo et al., 2005; Goode and Eck, 2007) models assume that an open end of the filament has the natural 167° helical twist that is favorable for adding a subunit.
evidence: This is a description of assumptions in some models from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Most models assume a rapid equilibrium between open and closed states but differ in detail.
source: Most models assume a rapid equilibrium between open and closed states but differ in detail.
evidence: This is a summary of existing models in the literature.

claim: The original crystal structure of the Bni1 FH2 dimer suggested that the trailing FH2 domain sterically blocks subunit addition.
source: The original crystal structure of the Bni1 FH2 dimer (Xu et al., 2004) suggested that the trailing FH2 domain sterically blocks subunit addition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of a crystal structure supported by citation.

claim: The structure of Bni1 FH2 domains bound to actin with a 180° twist revealed that FH2 domains can not only interfere sterically with elongation but also distort the filament into flattened helical twists > 167° that are unfavorable for subunit addition.
source: The structure of Bni1 FH2 domains bound to actin with a 180° twist (Otomo et al., 2005) revealed that FH2 domains can not only interfere sterically with elongation but also distort the filament into flattened helical twists > 167° that are unfavorable for subunit addition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of a crystal structure supported by citation.

claim: Homology models of Cdc12 and mDia1 FH2 domains were created based on the crystal structure of the Bni1 FH2 domain.
source: We created homology models of Cdc12 and mDia1 FH2 domains based on the crystal structure of the Bni1 FH2 domain and used Baker's model of the Bni1 FH2-actin filament (Baker et al., 2015) to align these FH2 models on the end of a filament consisting of seven subunits (see the Materials and methods section for details).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The FH2-actin complexes were solvated, ionized and then refined by extensive AA MD simulations.
source: The FH2-actin complexes were solvated, ionized and then refined by extensive AA MD simulations (Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: At the end of the 200 ns simulations, the total energies of the three models of formin dimers interacting with actin filaments were within the range of protein structures in the PDB determined by X-ray crystallography and NMR.
source: At the end of the 200 ns simulations, the total energies of the three models of formin dimers interacting with actin filaments (calculated by ProSA [Wiederstein and Sippl, 2007]) were within the range of protein structures in the PDB determined by X-ray crystallography and NMR (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a validation of the homology models based on energy calculations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Bni1 model (z-score = −8.9) is the most accurate.
source: The z-scores indicate that the Bni1 model (z-score = −8.9) is the most accurate (as it is based on a crystal structure), and Cdc12 (z-score = −7.69) is more accurate than mDia1 (z-score = −6.45), because the sequence of the Bni1 template model is more similar to the Cdc12 model than the mDia1 model.
evidence: This is an assessment of model quality based on z-scores calculated from the simulations.

claim: Cdc12 (z-score = −7.69) is more accurate than mDia1 (z-score = −6.45).
source: The z-scores indicate that the Bni1 model (z-score = −8.9) is the most accurate (as it is based on a crystal structure), and Cdc12 (z-score = −7.69) is more accurate than mDia1 (z-score = −6.45), because the sequence of the Bni1 template model is more similar to the Cdc12 model than the mDia1 model.
evidence: This is an assessment of model quality based on z-scores and sequence similarity.

claim: The models of the three formin/actin systems obtained from the AA simulations are very similar.
source: The models of the three formin/actin systems obtained from the AA simulations are very similar (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All three models have the FHL and FHT positioned head-to-tail to form a donut-like shape around the barbed end of an actin filament with seven subunits.
source: All three models have the FHL (leading FH2 domain) and FHT (trailing FH2 domain) positioned head-to-tail to form a donut-like shape around the barbed end of an actin filament with seven subunits (Otomo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the simulations, consistent with previous structural work.

claim: Each FH2 subunit consists of helical knob and post regions connected by a three-helix bundle (coiled-coil).
source: Each FH2 subunit consists of helical knob and post regions connected by a three-helix bundle (coiled-coil).
evidence: This is a structural description from the simulation models.

claim: The N-terminal lasso region of each subunit encircles the post of the other subunit and is connected to the knob of its own subunit by a flexible linker.
source: The N-terminal lasso region of each subunit encircles the post of the other subunit and is connected to the knob of its own subunit by a flexible linker (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a structural description from the simulation models shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The coiled-coil and post regions of the FH2 domains of the three formins align quite well.
source: The coiled-coil and post regions of the FH2 domains of the three formins align quite well (Figure 2E), while other regions differ locally (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: The lasso regions of the FH2 domains have similar circular conformations, but the mDia1 FH2 lasso lacks a helix found in Cdc12 and Bni1.
source: The lasso regions of the FH2 domains have similar circular conformations, but the mDia1 FH2 lasso lacks a helix found in Cdc12 and Bni1.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models.

claim: The helical parts of the linker regions align quite well with each other, but the unstructured parts differ in length and conformation.
source: The helical parts of the linker regions align quite well with each other, but the unstructured parts differ in length and conformation.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models.

claim: The knob regions align the least well among the three formins.
source: The knob regions align the least well.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models.

claim: The mDia1 knob has fewer helices than the Cdc12 and Bni1 knobs.
source: The mDia1 knob has fewer helices than the Cdc12 and Bni1 knobs.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models.

claim: The locations of the helices and loops in the mDia1 knobs differ much more than those in the knobs of the other two formins.
source: Also, the locations of the helices and loops in the mDia1 knobs differ much more than those in the knobs of the other two formins.
evidence: This is a structural comparison from the simulation models.

claim: During the remainder of the 500 ns AA simulations, steric interference with subunit +A1 increased for Cdc12 and decreased for mDia1, with Bni1 in between.
source: During the remainder of the 500 ns AA simulations, steric interference with subunit +A1 increased for Cdc12 and decreased for mDia1, with Bni1 in between (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the AA simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During two rounds of AA simulations of five-mer filaments lacking subunit A1, the steric interference of FHT with the site where subunit A1 binds increased to high levels for Cdc12 and fluctuated between none and low levels for Bni1 and mDia1.
source: During two rounds of AA simulations of five-mer filaments lacking subunit A1, the steric interference of FHT with the site where subunit A1 binds increased to high levels for Cdc12 and fluctuated between none and low levels for Bni1 and mDia1 (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the AA simulations shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The fractions of the time when FHT occupied >1% of the volume fraction of A1 in the two replicates were 64% and 21% for Cdc12, 19% and 18% for Bni1 and 4% and 2% for mDia1.
source: The fractions of the time when FHT occupied >1% of the volume fraction of A1 in the two replicates (350 ns for the first replicate and 200 ns for the second replicate) were, respectively, 64% and 21% for Cdc12, 19% and 18% for Bni1 and 4% and 2% for mDia1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the AA simulations.

claim: Both FHL and FHT of Cdc12 created more steric interference for subunit addition than Bni1 or mDia1.
source: Thus, both FHL and FHT of Cdc12 created more steric interference for subunit addition than Bni1 or mDia1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the steric interference measurements in the simulations.

claim: During the first 100 ns of the simulations with each of the formins, the root mean-squared deviations (RMSD) of the alpha-carbon atoms changed before stabilizing.
source: During the first 100 ns of the simulations with each of the formins, the root mean-squared deviations (RMSD) of the alpha-carbon atoms changed before stabilizing (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation trajectories shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Bni1 FH2-actin complex changed the most during the first 100 ns.
source: The Bni1 FH2-actin complex changed the most during this time (Figure 2D, from Baker et al. [Baker et al., 2015]), since the model actin filament started with a 167° twist and the FH2 contacts came from a co-crystal structure with a 180° twist of the actin helix.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation trajectories with an explanation based on the initial model structure.

claim: In the Baker simulations of Bni1 FH2 domains, the twist angle relaxed from 167° to ~172°.
source: In the Baker simulations of Bni1 FH2 domains (Baker et al., 2015), the twist angle relaxed from 167° to ~172°, the conformation used here for the homology models of Cdc12 and mDia1 FH2 domains.
evidence: This is a finding from previous simulations cited in the manuscript.

claim: The RMSDs of filaments with Cdc12 and mDia1 FH2 domains changed less than Bni1 during the first 100 ns of simulations.
source: The RMSDs of these filaments with Cdc12 and mDia1 FH2 domains changed less than Bni1 during the first 100 ns of simulations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation trajectories shown in Figure 2D.

claim: During the subsequent 400 ns of AA MD simulations, the actin filament seven-mer with mDia1 FH2 relaxed toward twist angles more favorable for binding an incoming actin subunit than filaments with Bni1 or Cdc12.
source: During the subsequent 400 ns of AA MD simulations, the actin filament seven-mer with mDia1 FH2 relaxed toward twist angles more favorable for binding an incoming actin subunit than filaments with Bni1 or Cdc12 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the AA simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The twist angles between the first two pairs of subunits of all three samples decreased continuously from ~172° as they fluctuated on shorter time scales.
source: The twist angles between the first two pairs of subunits of all three samples decreased continuously from ~172° (Figure 4D,F) as they fluctuated on shorter time scales (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the AA simulations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The angles between the first and second pairs of actin subunits were strongly correlated.
source: The angles between the first and second pairs of actin subunits were strongly correlated.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data.

claim: After 500 ns of simulations, the twist angles of the terminal actin subunits associated with the mDia1 FH2 (twistA1-A2 = 169.4°±0.7° and twistA2-A3 = 167.2°±1.1°) were close to 167°.
source: After 500 ns of simulations, the twist angles of the terminal actin subunits associated with the mDia1 FH2 (twistA1-A2 = 169.4°±0.7° and twistA2-A3 = 167.2°±1.1°, means ± SD) were close to 167° while those associated with Cdc12 (twistA1-A2 = 171.3° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 169.6° ± 0.5°) or Bni1 (twistA1-A2 = 170.7° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 170.2° ± 0.5°) FH2 fluctuated mostly in the angle range of 169–173° (Figure 4E,G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the AA simulations shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: The twist angles associated with Cdc12 (twistA1-A2 = 171.3° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 169.6° ± 0.5°) or Bni1 (twistA1-A2 = 170.7° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 170.2° ± 0.5°) FH2 fluctuated mostly in the angle range of 169–173°.
source: After 500 ns of simulations, the twist angles of the terminal actin subunits associated with the mDia1 FH2 (twistA1-A2 = 169.4°±0.7° and twistA2-A3 = 167.2°±1.1°, means ± SD) were close to 167° while those associated with Cdc12 (twistA1-A2 = 171.3° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 169.6° ± 0.5°) or Bni1 (twistA1-A2 = 170.7° ± 0.4° and twistA2-A3 = 170.2° ± 0.5°) FH2 fluctuated mostly in the angle range of 169–173° (Figure 4E,G).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the AA simulations shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: The angles between subunits further from the barbed end were more variable during the 500 ns AA simulations.
source: The angles between subunits further from the barbed end were more variable during the 500 ns AA simulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The pointed end subunits were close to 167° on average as they are in the middle of long actin filaments, but they varied more over time due to the presence of fewer neighboring subunits.
source: The pointed end subunits (twist angles between A6-A7 and A5-A6) were close to 167° on average as they are in the middle of long actin filaments, but they varied more over time due to the presence of fewer neighboring subunits.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data with an explanation based on structural constraints.

claim: The FH2 domains of Cdc12 and Bni1 only flattened the end of the filament locally.
source: Therefore, the FH2 domains of Cdc12 and Bni1 only flattened the end of the filament locally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the twist angle measurements in the simulations.

claim: Two separate AA simulations of five-mer filaments revealed that each of the three formin FH2 domains favors distinctly different twist angles between subunits A2 and A3.
source: Two separate AA simulations of five-mer filaments revealed that each of the three formin FH2 domains favors distinctly different twist angles between subunits A2 and A3, the two subunits that form the binding site for incoming subunit A1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the AA simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The most probable twist angles in the two replicates were 168.2° ± 0.5° and 170.3° ± 0.7° for mDia1, 172.2° ± 0.8° and 171.6° ± 1.2° for Bni1 and 173.9° ± 0.8° and 175.1° ± 0.7° for Cdc12.
source: The most probable twist angles in the two replicates were 168.2° ± 0.5° and 170.3° ± 0.7° for mDia1, 172.2° ± 0.8° and 171.6° ± 1.2° for Bni1 and 173.9° ± 0.8° and 175.1° ± 0.7° for Cdc12 (Figure 5B,C) with fluctuations for each over a range of about 4°.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the AA simulations shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The maximum difference in the twist angles at the actin barbed ends interacting with Cdc12 and mDia1 reached up to 9° during these simulations.
source: The maximum difference in the twist angles at the actin barbed ends interacting with Cdc12 and mDia1 reached up to 9° during these simulations.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the AA simulations.

claim: mDia1 FH2 favored the 'open' configuration of barbed ends awaiting the association of a subunit.
source: Therefore, mDia1 FH2 favored the 'open' configuration of barbed ends awaiting the association of a subunit, while Cdc12 favored twist angles that compromise subunit addition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the twist angle measurements in the simulations.

claim: Cdc12 favored twist angles that compromise subunit addition.
source: Therefore, mDia1 FH2 favored the 'open' configuration of barbed ends awaiting the association of a subunit, while Cdc12 favored twist angles that compromise subunit addition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the twist angle measurements in the simulations.

claim: The 80 ns MB-MetaD simulations confirmed that mDia1 FH2 favored 'open' twist angles near 168°, while the Cdc12 FH2 favored the 'closed' twist angles > 170°.
source: The 80 ns MB-MetaD simulations confirmed that mDia1 FH2 favored 'open' twist angles near 168°, while the Cdc12 FH2 favored the 'closed' twist angles > 170° (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a finding from the MB-MetaD simulations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Bni1 FH2 favored intermediate twist angles but the distribution resembled mDia1 more than Cdc12.
source: The Bni1 FH2 favored intermediate twist angles but the distribution resembled mDia1 more than Cdc12.
evidence: This is a finding from the MB-MetaD simulations.

claim: During the last 20 ns of the 200 ns AA simulations, contacts between the FH2 domains and actin filament buried the following total surface areas: Cdc12 total 10,725 Å2; Bni1 total 10,116 Å2; and mDia1 total 10,573 Å2.
source: During the last 20 ns of the 200 ns AA simulations, contacts between the FH2 domains and actin filament buried the following total surface areas: Cdc12 FHL 5493 ± 341 Å2 (mean ± SD), Cdc12 FHT 5232 ± 207 Å2, Cdc12 total 10,725 Å2; Bni1 FHL 4752 ± 205 Å2, Bni1 FHT 5364 ± 247 Å2, Bni1 total 10,116 Å2; and mDia1 FHL 4938 ± 212 Å2, mDia1 FHT 5635 ± 250 Å2, mDia1 total 10,573 Å2.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the AA simulations.

claim: The differences in buried surface area do not correlate with the gating factors.
source: Thus, the differences in buried surface area do not correlate with the gating factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing buried surface area measurements with known gating factors.

claim: FHT made more contacts than FHL, because of the presence of the terminal subunit A1 in seven-mer filaments.
source: FHT made more contacts than FHL, because of the presence of the terminal subunit A1 in seven-mer filaments.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data with an explanation based on the model structure.

claim: The lasso, linker, knob and post regions of both FH2 domains of all three formins contributed to contacts with the actin filament.
source: The lasso, linker, knob and post regions of both FH2 domains of all three formins contributed to these contacts with the actin filament, with major contacts between FHT and A1 and A3 and between FHL and A2.
evidence: This is an observation from the contact analysis of the simulations.

claim: Mutations of formin FMNL3 K800A and R782A in the post and R570A in the lasso slowed actin filament elongation, presumably by decreasing the gating factor of ~0.4.
source: Mutations of formin FMNL3 had implicated the post and lasso regions in gating: mutations K800A and R782A in the post and R570A in the lasso slowed actin filament elongation, presumably by decreasing the gating factor of ~0.4 (Thompson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from previous experimental work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The knob regions made the most extensive contacts with actin filaments, especially with the barbed end grooves of subunits A2 (by FHL) and A3 (by FHT).
